EUROPE's gas stocks in record seasonal slump

Europe’s gas prices are surging as a sudden stratospheric warming event and weakening polar vortex allow colder arctic air to penetrate the region and upend widespread expectations of a mild start to the winter heating season.

Benchmark gas futures prices have surged back towards their highest in almost four years as the amount of gas in storage has fallen at the fastest rate on record for the time of year.

Front-month futures in the Dutch TTF contract climbed to €92 per megawatt-hour on November 12 and were three times higher than €30 on the same date a year ago.

Combined inventories of gas across the European Union and the United Kingdom plunged by 43 terawatt-hours (TWh) between October 27 and November 11.

Underground storage emptied at more than four times the average rate of 10 TWh over the same period in the last ten years.

The run down compared with a depletion of just 5 TWh in 2025 and easily exceeded the prior record of 38 TWh set in 2016 ...

COP31: Campaigners reject nuclear energy as climate solution

Campaigners at the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31) have rejected nuclear energy as a solution to the global energy and climate crisis.

The campaigners, who staged a protest at the Blue Zone of the COP31 venue in Antalya, Turkey, holding aloft placards and banners bearing messages such as “Nuclear is no solution,” called for increased investment in renewable energy sources, particularly solar and wind power.

Copper slides to four-month low as AI concerns and Fed outlook weigh

Copper is heading for a fifth consecutive weekly decline, with futures in London and New York both falling to four-month lows amid growing turmoil in the artificial intelligence sector and mounting expectations of further US interest rate hikes. The crisis engulfing Nvidia, the influential chipmaker at the centre of the AI boom, has cast doubt on the scale and pace of future AI infrastructure investment. This has undermined one of copper's key bullish demand narratives, with investors increasingly questioning whether the massive spending planned for data centres, power grids and related infrastructure will materialise as expected.

Meanwhile, a stronger dollar and rising US Treasury yields, driven by persistent inflation and an increasingly hawkish Fed outlook, have added further pressure on industrial metals. COMEX high-grade copper futures briefly touched USD 6.1165 per pound, marking a nearly 12% reversal from September's record high. The decline has brought prices below the 200-day moving average, with a sustained break potentially opening the door to further losses towards USD 5.93, the 38.2% Fibonacci retracement of the broader rally shown in the chart. 

While the technical outlook has weakened, attracting long liquidation from funds, longer-term electrification and grid investment needs remain intact, suggesting the current selloff reflects a reassessment of near-term growth expectations rather than a fundamental reversal of copper's structural demand outlook.

Exchange stocks rise modestly, but China remains exceptionally tight

Copper inventories monitored by the three major futures exchanges rose by a modest 4,860 tonnes over the past week to 1.088 million tonnes, remaining elevated by historical standards. The increase was driven by a 12,400-tonne build in LME warehouses to 329,000 tonnes, partly offset by a 1,300-tonne decline in COMEX stocks, the first weekly withdrawal since April.

More importantly, Shanghai Futures Exchange inventories fell by another 6,200 tonnes to just 27,600 tonnes, their lowest level in nearly three years. The continued drawdown highlights persistent tightness in China's physical copper market, contrasting sharply with the relatively comfortable inventory situation elsewhere.

This divergence is also reflected in elevated domestic spot premiums and the premiums Chinese buyers are willing to pay for imported copper relative to LME prices. While the broader market is increasingly focused on weakening investment sentiment and the potential slowdown in AI-related demand, China's exceptionally low inventories provide an important counterweight to the bearish narrative. The growing geographical imbalance in available stocks suggests that global headline inventory figures may overstate the amount of metal readily available to meet demand in the world's largest copper-consuming market.

#Commodities: 
The Bloomberg Commodity Total Return Index is heading for a fourth consecutive, albeit modest, weekly decline, slipping to a three-month low and reducing its year-to-date gain to 26%. All sectors except grains trades lower, led by metals, with precious metals down 4% in response to a stronger dollar and a 35-basis-point jump in the US two-year Treasury yield, driven by another hotter-than-expected CPI report and hawkish Fed commentary, dominated sentiment. Meanwhile, continued weakness in crude oil and refined products was partly offset by renewed strength in natural gas. Grains bucked the broader downtrend, rebounding after weeks of speculative long liquidation. Wheat found support from faltering Russia–Ukraine peace talks, while corn and soybeans rallied following a USDA report pointing to tighter-than-expected US supplies.

Metals: Gold tumbled to USD 3,852 on Thursday, a 13-month low, before staging a modest rebound during the Asian session to trade near USD 3,900. Bullion is down more than 4% on the week, with sentiment deteriorating following another hotter-than-expected US CPI print that drove bond yields and the dollar higher while reinforcing expectations of more aggressive Fed tightening.  For now, sentiment remains weak, with short sellers firmly in control. In our view, a recovery above USD 4,000 is needed to ease the downside pressure and signal a potential shift in momentum.

Oil: Brent trades higher for a third consecutive day, hovering near USD 96.50, as prospects for a deal to end the US–Iran conflict remain elusive. President Trump has ruled out the need for an agreement with Tehran, instead directing Vice President Vance to focus on domestic priorities. Iran, meanwhile, continues to demand an end to the US naval blockade and sanctions while refusing to surrender its enriched nuclear material. Despite the rebound, crude is heading for a second consecutive, albeit smaller, weekly decline as Middle East crude exports recover towards pre-war levels. However, flows of refined products and natural gas remain constrained, an important distinction given that these markets continue to face the most acute supply disruptions and price pressures.
